subtitle: Look at well-being as part of doing the work well over time. Recognize early signs that your pace is not working, use small protections, ask for support early and know where support lives.
audience: For all DHS and DSD staff. It offers ideas you can use as you choose. It does not measure anyone's well-being, ask you to share anything personal or replace health care, counseling or HR guidance.

lessons.title: Why well-being belongs at work
objectives: Explain why well-being is part of doing the job well over time, not a perk.
Describe well-being as shared between personal habits and the conditions of work.
Name the five essentials in the U.S. Surgeon General's framework for workplace mental health and well-being.
Describe meaning in the work as a source of energy that can be noticed and protected.
lessons.teaching:
How people feel at work shapes how they treat the people they serve, their colleagues and themselves. A rested case manager listens better, catches more and makes steadier decisions. Well-being is not a reward for finishing the work. It is part of being able to keep doing it.

Well-being is shared. Personal habits matter: sleep, breaks, time with people who matter to you. So do the conditions of work: caseload, staffing, schedules and how a team runs. This course covers both. It never asks you to fix alone what the work itself needs to fix.

The U.S. Surgeon General's 2022 Framework for Workplace Mental Health and Well-Being names five essentials: protection from harm, connection and community, work-life harmony, mattering at work, and opportunity for growth. Worker voice and equity sit at the center. The framework is written mainly for employers and leaders, and it is a useful checklist for anyone thinking about what a healthy workplace provides.

Most people came to human services work for a reason. Remembering that reason, and noticing when the work still delivers it, is one of the strongest supports there is. A thank-you from a family, a problem solved with a colleague, a process made fairer: these moments are worth noticing on purpose.
lessons.keyPoint: Well-being is part of doing good work over the long run. It is shared between personal habits and the conditions of work.
lessons.example: Practice case: The case manager has carried a full caseload for two years and is good at it. Lately the case manager answers email at 10 p.m., skips lunch and feels flat even after a good outcome for a family.
lessons.question: Which description of the situation is most useful?
choices: The case manager needs to be more resilient.
The case manager's pace and the workload both deserve a look, and the case manager can start with one small change.
This is normal for the job, so nothing needs to change.
feedback: Personal resilience helps, and framing it this way puts the whole problem on one person and ignores the workload.
This keeps both parts in view: what the case manager can try now, and what the workload needs. Neither has to wait for the other.
Heavy seasons happen, and feeling flat after good news is a signal worth noticing, not something to accept as normal.
lessons.reflection: What part of your work still gives you energy? When did you last notice it?
lessons.action: Read the five essentials in the Surgeon General's framework. Pick the one your team does best and the one that most needs attention. Keep notes private unless you choose to share them.

check.question: According to this course, who is responsible for well-being at work?
check.correct: It is shared: individuals can use personal habits, and leaders shape workload, staffing and how the team runs.
wrong: Only the individual employee, through self-care.
Only the agency, so individual habits do not matter.
check.feedback: Both parts matter. Personal habits help, and the conditions of work often matter more. Supervisors and managers carry more of that responsibility because they control workload and schedules.

lessons.title: Sustainable pace and early signs
objectives: Define a sustainable pace as one you could keep for a year, with recovery between heavier periods.
Recognize common early signs that a pace is not working.
Describe the World Health Organization's description of burnout as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical diagnosis.
Choose a response to after-hours work that protects recovery time for yourself and others.
lessons.teaching:
A sustainable pace is one you could keep for a year. Some weeks will be heavier: a deadline, a staffing gap, a crisis in a family's life. The question is whether you recover between them. A pace that only works if nothing else goes wrong is not sustainable.

Early signs often show up before anyone names them. A shorter temper. Trouble switching off in the evening. Dreading tasks you used to like. Feeling numb after good news. These are signals, not failures, and noticing them early gives you more options.

The World Health Organization describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon that results from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. It names three dimensions: exhaustion, increased mental distance from or negative feelings about one's job, and reduced professional efficacy. The WHO is clear that burnout refers to the work context and is not classified as a medical condition. This course is not a diagnostic tool. If you are concerned about your health, talk with a health care provider.

After-hours work is a common pressure point. Answering a non-urgent email at 10 p.m. clears the inbox, and it also teaches everyone, you included, that evenings are work time. Scheduling the reply for the morning keeps the work off other people's evenings too.
lessons.keyPoint: A sustainable pace is one you could keep for a year. Early signs are signals, not failures.
lessons.example: Practice case: It is 9:45 p.m. The case manager sees a non-urgent email from a colleague asking about next week's schedule.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do?
choices: Answer it now so it is done.
Write a reply and schedule it to send at 8 a.m.
feedback: It clears the inbox, and it teaches everyone, the case manager included, that evenings are work time.
Nothing is lost, and the case manager gets real time off. This is a good choice.
A good middle path if the case manager wants it off their mind. It keeps the work off the evening for the colleague, too.
lessons.reflection: What are your own early signs that your pace is not working? Who or what usually notices first?
lessons.action: Choose one after-hours habit to change for two weeks, such as a fixed time you stop checking email, and notice what happens.

check.question: How does the World Health Organization describe burnout?
check.correct: As an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed.
wrong: As a medical diagnosis that requires treatment.
As a personal weakness that affects people who are not committed.
check.feedback: The WHO classifies burnout as an occupational phenomenon tied to work, not as a medical condition, and it is never a sign of weak commitment.

lessons.title: Small protections and asking early
objectives: Name small protections that add up over time.
Explain how boundaries also protect the people a team serves.
Raise a workload concern early, with facts.
Distinguish asking for support from admitting failure.
lessons.teaching:
Small protections add up. A real lunch break away from the screen. A fixed time you stop checking email. A five-minute pause after a hard call before the next one. Walking to a colleague's desk instead of sending one more message. None of these fixes a heavy workload, and all of them help you meet it.

Boundaries serve the people we serve too. A case manager who has recovered catches the detail in a file, hears what a parent is really asking and makes a steadier call. Protecting your time is part of protecting the quality of the work.

It is easier to adjust a workload, a schedule or a deadline before a crisis than after one. Asking early is a skill. Bring facts: how your caseload has changed, what is slipping, and what would help most. A supervisor can act on "my caseload is up a third since spring and two reports are now late" in a way they cannot act on "I'm swamped."

Asking is not admitting failure. Workload is a shared responsibility, and a supervisor who hears early has more options: moving a case, adjusting a deadline, asking for help from another unit. Waiting until something breaks leaves fewer choices for everyone.
lessons.keyPoint: Ask early, with facts. A supervisor has more options before a crisis than after one.
lessons.example: Practice case: The case manager's caseload has grown by a third since spring. Two monthly reports are late. The case manager has not mentioned it to the supervisor.
lessons.question: What should the case manager do?
choices: Keep going, since everyone is busy.
Raise it with the supervisor and bring the numbers.
Start looking for another job without saying anything.
feedback: Common, and the cost builds quietly until it shows up in the work or in the case manager's health.
Asking early, with facts, gives the supervisor something to act on. This is the strongest choice.
That may be the right choice in the end, and the team never gets the chance to fix the workload.
lessons.reflection: What makes it hard for you to ask for support at work? What would make it easier?
lessons.action: Write the three facts you would bring to a workload conversation: what has changed, what is slipping and what would help most.

check.question: Which request gives a supervisor the most to act on?
check.correct: "My caseload is up a third since spring and two reports are late. Could we move two cases or adjust the report deadline?"
wrong: "Everyone is overloaded, so there is no point asking."
check.feedback: Facts and a specific request make it possible to act. A general statement is honest, and it leaves the supervisor guessing.

lessons.title: Supporting a colleague and where support lives
objectives: Check in with a colleague privately and without pressure.
Describe where support lives, including the state Employee Assistance Program.
Know how to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and when to call 911.
Plan one small protection to try for two weeks.
lessons.teaching:
You can support a colleague without fixing anything. Notice, ask and listen. "You've seemed stretched lately. How are you doing?" said privately, gives the other person room to share as much or as little as they want. You do not need to diagnose or solve. You can listen and point to support.

Find out where support lives before you need it. Your supervisor can adjust workload and schedules. For State of Minnesota employees, LifeMatters is the Employee Assistance Program. Minnesota Management and Budget describes it as free, voluntary and confidential counseling and life support for state employees and the people they live with, with a stated legal exception to confidentiality for serious safety concerns. Your agency's leave and flexibility options are another route. HR can explain them.

If you are struggling to cope, or thinking about harming yourself, reach out now. In the United States you can call or text 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or chat at 988lifeline.org. You do not need to be in crisis to talk to someone. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.

Good work over the long run needs people who can keep doing it. Everyone can look out for each other. Supervisors and managers control workload and schedules, so they carry more of the responsibility for a sustainable pace.
lessons.keyPoint: Notice, ask and listen. You do not need to fix it. You can point to support.
lessons.example: Practice case: The new colleague notices the case manager has seemed withdrawn in meetings for a few weeks and left early twice without saying goodbye.
lessons.question: What should the new colleague do?
choices: Say nothing, since it is not the new colleague's business.
Ask privately, "How are you doing? You've seemed stretched lately."
Mention it to the whole team so everyone can help.
feedback: Respecting privacy matters, and a kind, private check-in does not invade it.
Simple and caring. The case manager can share as much or as little as they want, and the new colleague can mention support options if it seems right.
Well meant, and it puts the case manager on the spot in front of others.
lessons.reflection: Who checks in on you at work? Who might be glad if you checked in on them?
lessons.action: Look up your Employee Assistance Program contact information and save it where you can find it quickly. Then pick one small protection to try for the next two weeks.

check.question: A colleague tells you they have been thinking about not wanting to be alive. What is the right step?
check.correct: Stay with them, encourage them to call or text 988 now, and call 911 if they are in immediate danger.
wrong: Promise to keep it secret and check in next week.
Tell them to take some time off and rest.
check.feedback: Thoughts of suicide need support now. The 988 Lifeline is available by call or text, and 911 is for immediate danger. Do not promise secrecy when someone's safety is at risk.

An occupational phenomenon from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Not a medical diagnosis.
Protection from harm, connection and community, work-life harmony, mattering at work, opportunity for growth, with worker voice and equity at the center.
Bring what has changed, what is slipping and what would help most.
Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. Call 911 for immediate danger.
